# Git Merge vs Git Rebase

## What They Do

**Merge** joins two branches by creating a new "merge commit" that has two parents:
```
main:    A---B---C---M
                    /
feature:    D---E--
```
The history shows exactly when branches diverged and rejoined.

**Rebase** moves your commits to sit on top of another branch, rewriting their history:
```
Before:          After rebase onto main:
main:  A---B---C    main:  A---B---C
              \                    \
feature: D---E  feature:    D'---E'
```
D and E become new commits (D', E') with new hashes.

---

## Key Differences

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserves exact history | Creates linear history |
| Commits | Adds a merge commit | Rewrites existing commits |
| Safety | Safe on shared branches | **Dangerous on shared branches** |
| Conflicts | Resolve once | Resolve per-commit |
| Traceability | Easy to see branch points | Harder to see original context |

---

## When to Use Each

### Use **Merge** when:
- Working on **shared/public branches** (main, develop)
- You want to **preserve the true history** of what happened
- Merging a completed feature branch into main
- Working with a team where others have pulled the branch

```bash
git checkout main
git merge feature/my-feature
```

### Use **Rebase** when:
- **Updating your local feature branch** with recent changes from main
- You want a **clean, linear history** before merging
- Cleaning up messy local commits before sharing
- Your branch only exists on your machine

```bash
git checkout feature/my-feature
git rebase main
```

---

## The Golden Rule

> **Never rebase a branch that others are working on**

Rebasing rewrites commit hashes. If someone else has based work on your original commits, their history becomes incompatible with yours — causing painful conflicts.

---

## Common Workflows

### Option 1: Merge everything
```bash
# Simple, safe, noisy history
git checkout main && git merge feature
```

### Option 2: Rebase then merge (most popular)
```bash
# Clean up your branch first, then merge cleanly
git checkout feature
git rebase main          # update with latest main
git checkout main
git merge feature        # now a fast-forward, no merge commit
```

### Option 3: Interactive rebase (clean up before sharing)
```bash
# Squash/edit your commits before merging
git rebase -i main
```
This lets you squash "WIP" commits, fix typos in messages, etc.

---

## Quick Decision Guide

```
Is the branch public/shared?
├── Yes → Use MERGE
└── No (local only)
    ├── Want clean linear history? → REBASE
    └── Want to preserve history? → MERGE
```

The most practical default: **rebase your local feature branches onto main to stay updated, then merge (or PR) into main when done.**
